data.title: Meta settles claims with second plaintiff in social media addiction case
data.description: Meta on Friday reached a settlement with a teen plaintiff, identified in court documents as K.D.B., who claimed the company’s platforms, Instagram and Facebook, were addictive and caused her mental ‌health problems, attorneys for the plaintiff said. The news comes just one day after the tech giant reached a settlement with S.J., the second teen plaintiff who had sued the company over similar claims. The terms of the settlement agreements with both plaintiffs are confidential. In the weeks leading up to trial, TikTok and YouTube reached agreements to resolve the claims brought against them by both S.J. and K.D.B. “We remain committed to improving safety for kids on social media apps and holding tech companies accountable, and we are pleased to have brought this matter to a just resolution on behalf of our client,” Emily Jeffcott, trial counsel for K.D.B., said in a statement. Snap Inc. now remains the lone defendant in the trial, which began this week in Los Angeles with jury selection. Opening arguments are slated for Nov. 4. In their lawsuit, K.D.B. and S.J. allege that Snap, the maker of Snapchat, designed features that would maximize the time young users spend on the app. Those features include Snapstreaks, Snapscores and filters that can trigger compulsive use of Snapchat, leading to severe mental and physical health issues like self-harm. Their case is the fourth bellweather in a consolidated group of cases brought against Instagram, YouTube, TikTok and Snap by more than 1,600 plaintiffs, including over 350 families and over 250 school districts. The plaintiffs accuse the tech companies of knowingly designing addictive products harmful to young users’ mental health. Historically, social media platforms have largely been shielded by Section 230, a provision added to the Communications Act of 1934 that says internet companies aren’t liable for the content users post. Meta, which owns Instagram and Facebook, has repeatedly denied that its apps are purposefully harmful and addictive for young users. In March, during a landmark social media addiction trial in Los Angeles, a jury found Meta and Google’s YouTube negligent in the design or operation of their social media platforms. The jurors determined that Meta’s and Google’s negligence were a substantial factor in causing harm to the plaintiff, identified in court by her initials, K.G.M., and that the companies failed to adequately warn users of the dangers of Instagram and YouTube, their respective platforms. It awarded K.G.M. $3 million in compensatory damages, finding Meta 70% responsible for harm caused to the now 20-year-old plaintiff, and YouTube responsible for 30%. In August, Meta agreed to settle a wide-ranging social media addiction lawsuit with the state of California and a number of other states for about $18 billion. The court filing says that the company “denies the allegations against it and that it has any liability to the Plaintiffs,” which are a collection of 29 states. In a statement to NBC News on Friday, a spokesperson for Meta said the company will continue to defend itself in court and stand by its record. “We’ve spent more than a decade building protections for teens, and our agreement with 52 bipartisan attorneys general goes even further with strict time limits, no access at night, and no notifications during school hours,” the statement read in part. “We hope the rest of our industry joins us in setting this new standard.” A spokesperson for Snap on Friday sent NBC News its statement from earlier this week, which read, in part, “From the beginning, Snapchat was built differently from traditional social media: it opens to a camera, not a feed, not a ranking of what other people post or other social comparison metrics.” “We have built safeguards into the platform, introduced safety tools and educational resources,” the statement continued, “and we believe the evidence will support that we have put our community first, and that these allegations fundamentally misrepresent the plaintiffs’ experiences on Snapchat and how our platform was designed.”

data.title: ExxonMobil and Chevron report blowout profits as Trump touts benefits of high oil prices
data.description: It’s a good time to be an oil company. The two largest U.S. oil companies, ExxonMobil and Chevron, on Friday reported blowout profits that easily beat expectations as oil prices remain sharply elevated because of the U.S. war with Iran. ExxonMobil reported a profit that doubled from the same period last year, while Chevron’s earnings surged more than 180% from a year earlier. As part of the bumper returns, Exxon said it was increasing the dividend it pays to investors. The returns at both companies came as the price of oil surged beyond $100 per barrel and has remained there for months. On Friday, prices accelerated again, with Brent oil trading just under $118 per barrel. The highest level that Brent reached since the United States and Israel launched the Iran war in late February was $126, which it is now approaching again. Since the start of the year, Exxon shares have risen 52%, and Chevron shares have returned 50%. Overnight, another major oil company, BP, reported that its profit skyrocketed to an 18-year high. The average price of regular gasoline has soared 40% for consumers since the war broke out. Soaring prices continue to pressure consumers ahead of the midterm elections, where voters have repeatedly said that prices and inflation are primary concerns. In 2024, Donald Trump repeatedly pledged to drive energy costs down. “My plan will cut energy prices in half or more than that within 12 months of taking office,” the then-candidate said in September 2024, while adding that it would mean “gasoline below $2 a gallon.” As of Friday, the average gasoline price is currently more than double that. In recent rallies on the campaign trail, the president has celebrated the higher oil and gas profits. “I wonder if I should say this,” Trump mused aloud during a rally Oct. 24, before saying “our country is making hundreds of billions of dollars because of what’s happened in the Middle East.” “My people said, ‘Please don’t mention that, sir,’ because people are paying a little higher,” Trump continued. “But what we’ve done for this country, we’re making money like this country has never made before.” “I don’t give a damn: I’m going to say it. We’re making a freaking fortune.” The higher prices are also a result of the war between Ukraine and Russia following President Vladimir Putin’s full-scale invasion of his neighbor in 2022. “There’s a lot of disruption happening in the world,” ExxonMobil CEO Darren Woods told CNBC on Friday morning. “What you’re finding is because of the closure” in the Strait of Hormuz, “shipping has to find new routes around to continue to deliver the products that society desperately needs.” “About half of Russia’s refinery capacity has been taken out from the Ukraine bombing,” he added. “That shortage of refining capacity and availability to the world is what’s driving product prices as high as it is, and frankly, diesel is the key crunch point here because it is so critical to economic growth,” Woods continued. Since the start of the year, the average nationwide price for diesel fuel has risen 78%. New York-traded diesel futures have soared 130% since the start of the year, likely indicating more price rises could still come at the pump. Both Exxon and Chevron said that they were running their refineries at maximum output to continue making as much diesel as possible. Trump has taken specific note of the impact that diesel could have on the economy. The administration has quickly issued multiple orders and policies in an attempt to bring prices down. The president signed an order allowing more widespread use of an off-road dyed variety of diesel, has pressured European allies to release more of the diesel reserves into the global market, and has announced a deal with Putin for some of that country’s diesel supplies. Trump’s latest move came last week, when he announced $150 million in Defense Production Act funding to “expand petroleum production, storage, and logistics at refineries across.” The moves have not meaningfully brought prices down. On Friday, Woods said his refineries were already being pushed to the limit. “We are at record levels of utilization for our refineries,” he said on CNBC. “If you look at North America, we produce record volumes of diesel. That’s all been a function of trying to drive more product into the marketplace to meet that demand and to drive costs down.”

data.title: Binance pledges to cover billions in stolen assets after hack revives crypto fears
data.description: A record-setting cyberattack targeting the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange rocked the digital assets industry Friday, delivering another blow to a sector already struggling to achieve mainstream adoption. The exchange, Binance, announced late Thursday that more than $6 billion appeared to have moved through wallets connected to a security breach. Around $3 billion of that had potentially been located and frozen across several exchanges, though it was not immediately clear if those funds were recoverable. Early Friday, the company said it had set aside $5 billion to make affected users whole, and was working with partners to purchase an additional $1.34 billion to cover the total amount believed to have been stolen. The hack is the latest setback for crypto, which continues to reckon with a reputation for being too volatile — and too vulnerable to criminal activity — for widespread use. The scale of the hack echoes collapse of crypto exchange FTX, which, though not the result of a cyberattack, caused billions in losses. The renewed doubts were reflected in Bitcoin’s value Friday, which fell more than 5% overnight to approximately $77,000, accelerating its month-long downturn. Other affected cryptocurrencies fell as much as 9%. The crypto industry was already reeling from the failure in Congress of the Clarity Act, a bill that would have granted comprehensive legal protections for crypto assets in the U.S. Despite bipartisan support for the core elements of the legislation, its passage was torpedoed by a battle over conflict-of-interest rules for elected officials, notably President Donald Trump. The president has disclosed in filings that he earned more than $1 billion from crypto last year. The Binance hack stands to prolong this reckoning, experts said. “There will be an imperative for Binance to cover losses not only for its own reputation and value, but I expect there will be a level of co-operation within the space as they look at the collective reputational harm this may, rightly or wrongly, cause to the sector,” Laura Clatworthy, head of digital assets at Edwin Coe said in a statement. That cooperation was seen in the immediate reaction of other mainstream crypto players. Crypto firms Tether and Circle, which operate the two-largest stablecoins, worked quickly to freeze assets implicated in the hack. However, U.S. blockchain analysis firm TRM Labs estimates that $2.4 billion in Bitcoin and Ethereum will never be recovered. As of Friday morning, the hack’s origins remained murky. The whole heist unfolded in just 20 minutes starting at approximately 4 p.m. ET Thursday. Binance initially said the attack involved a compromised laptop. “However, our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach,” ‌it said in a statement on X, without elaborating. Multiple blockchain analysis firms said the hack had attributes associated with previous operations believed to have been carried out by North Korean actors. Binance co-CEO Richard Teng said Binance’s investigation had not yet identified the attackers. At least one prominent tech CEO could not resist making light of the situation. Elon Musk left a “yikes” emoji in response to an X user who noted that the collapsed crypto exchange FTX had initially also told users their funds were safe amid a wave of losses. Binance co-founder CZ Zhao responded:“Elon, have a lot of respect for you, but bad time to troll. Please stop.” Zhao noted that his SpaceX shares — the product of a Binance-related $500 million investment in Twitter, were now worth more than $1 billion. “Would appreciate if you show a little support. Thanks!”

data.title: Tech stocks set to wipe out $1 trillion in value as concerns about the AI boom deepen
data.description: Tech stocks plunged on Friday morning, putting the Nasdaq 100 index on course for a more than $1 trillion drop when the opening bell rings at 9:30 am ET in New York. Leading the declines were shares of Amazon, which fell 7%, and Intel, which plunged 26%. Both companies reported quarterly earnings this week that failed to reassure investors and analysts. Futures that track the broader S&P 500 also dropped sharply by more than 1.1%. As trillion-dollar tech companies raise and spend hundreds of billions of dollars to build massive artificial intelligence data centers and develop AI models, investors have been on edge as they look for clear signs that all this spending is actually delivering returns. On Thursday, Amazon reported that its spending to build out AI had continued at a faster clip than expected last quarter, while growth in its core online shopping business had slowed. The last time Amazon told investors it was upping it’s AI spending budget, the market rewarded the decision by sending shares up more than 15%. But a lot has changed in the past three months. Some of the big companies that pay to use AI models have tightened their token budgets. Others have raised questions about exactly how much benefit they’re getting from all the time and resources they’re putting into AI adoption. In response, some investors are now looking at big tech’s massive AI spending through a more skeptical lens. Nonetheless, Amazon CEO Andy Jassy told shareholders Thursday to brace for even more spending. “We still expect 2026 cash [capital expenditures] of approximately $220 billion, the majority for AWS, and expect to spend meaningfully more in 2027,” he said on the company’s earnings call. Amazon’s spending had already been set to double from 2025. Intel, meanwhile, told investors that its profits and sales in the fourth quarter would be lower than expected, which sent the stock tanking by 26%. Friday’s losses follow significant selling in shares of Alphabet on Thursday. The Google parent company shed about $500 billion in market value — its worst day ever and the second worst wipeout of value in market history. On Friday, the stock dropped another 1%. The Philadelphia semiconductor index, of which Intel is a member, sank 7% in pre-market trading on Friday. Other major chip shares followed Intel lower in pre-market trading. The ‘DRAM’ ETF, which tracks companies linked to computer memory and storage tumbled 6%. Intel’s stock has surged in recent months as its management implements a sweeping overhaul of the long-ailing chip firm. In the midst of that turnaround, the U.S. government took a stake in the company, making the federal government the company’s single largest shareholder. Even accounting for Friday’s expected drop, the value of the government’s stake in Intel has grown by 280%. Analysts at Citigroup called the described the report as “two steps forward, one step back.” A major issue highlighted by Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan that contributed to the company’s lackluster performance in the quarter were supply chain issues. “I’m disappointed that we were not able to meet strong customer demand in this quarter,” Tan told investors on the company’s earnings call. “We face near-term challenges, including manufacturing, supply shortage, the unprecedented memory crunch and the resulting softness in PC demand.” Meanwhile, one side effect of the selloff in tech shares was a rally in U.S. Treasuries. The tech companies that are borrowing hundreds of billions for AI data center buildouts have tapped the debt markets for funds, which appears to be creating a competition for capital. With those companies often offering better rates than the U.S. government, Treasury yields have, in part, risen in recent months. On Friday, the benchmark 10-year U.S. Treasury, which heavily influences consumer borrowing rates, fell from just under 5% on Thursday to around 4.89%.

data.title: Fears of Binance hack prompt Tether, Circle to freeze over $1.5 billion in funds
data.description: Cryptocurrency exchange Binance said Thursday it was investigating a “potential security issue” but insisted that all customer money was safe, after a series of very large transfers on the platform caught the attention of traders and the site’s founder speculated that it may have been due to a hack. “Our teams are aware of reports of a potential security issue and are actively investigating. Rest assured that user funds are completely safe,” a spokesperson for Binance said in a statement. “Our security teams are reviewing all relevant information with urgency,” the spokesperson said, urging users to “remain cautious of scams.” Binance is the world’s largest cryptocurrency trading platform by volume, with hundreds of thousands of users who buy, sell and store billions of dollars worth of digital currencies on the exchange. Unlike traditional bank deposits, money kept in accounts with companies like Binance is not insured by the government against losses, potentially leaving any refunds up to the discretion of individual exchanges. In the wake of Thursday’s reports, two major digital stablecoin issuers said they had taken steps to limit potential fallout if the Binance transfers turn out to be the result of a hacking attempt. Tether froze more than $1.567 billion worth of its digital currency “related to a potential Binance exchange hack,” CEO Paolo Ardoino said in a post on X. Jeremy Allaire, CEO of stablecoin issuer Circle. said the company had also frozen assets and was coordinating with law enforcement on the matter. “Circle is closely tracking reports of a potential exploit involving Binance. In coordination with law enforcement, we have frozen more than 800M USDC associated with the incident and will continue supporting the investigation,” he wrote, using the shorthand for the company’s United States Dollar Coin, whose value is pegged to the dollar. The sudden outflow from Binance, which was reported earlier by Bloomberg, occurred at a moment when cybersecurity defenses around the world are on high alert about the possibility of novel attacks facilitated by recent advances in artificial intelligence. Digital currency has been a primary target of hackers for years. In 2025, Coinbase disclosed that thieves had stolen customers’ personal information and attempted to extort the company for $20 million. Coinbase refused to pay and offered a bounty for information leading to arrests instead. Binance’s founder, Changpeng Zhao said, “It does look like a hack on Binance.” “As a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered,” he wrote on X, saying user funds “are safe.” Zhao stepped down as CEO of Binance in 2023 and pleaded guilty to breaking U.S. anti-money laundering laws. President Donald Trump later granted him a full pardon.

data.title: Chinese hackers used DeepSeek and other AI tools in sweeping global cyberattacks, report finds
data.description: Chinese state-linked hackers used artificial intelligence, including the popular DeepSeek model, to launch cyberattacks against more than 200 organizations around the world in just 11 days, according to the cybersecurity company CrowdStrike, in a campaign that illustrates how AI is allowing hackers to operate on a scale that previously required far more human effort.

data.title: Polymarket trading halted after vendor compromise; impacted users will be ‘made whole’
data.description: Predictions markets platform Polymarket was forced to halt trading on its international platform Thursday for nearly an hour because of what it said was a third-party compromise. There were also unconfirmed reports from users on Polymarket’s Discord channel who said their wallets had been drained. While Polymarket did not confirm that users had lost money, it said “anyone who has been impacted will be made whole.” “We’ll make this right and are fully reimbursing all affected traders,” the company said in a subsequent post on X. Crypto news website The Block reported some $2.65 million in cryptocurrencies had been siphoned from the platform, citing data from blockchain analysis group Arkham. In a statement posted on its X account, Polymarket said it had identified and fixed an issue affecting its international platform, Polymarket.com. “One of our 3rd party providers was compromised, and we have referred this to relevant law enforcement,” Polymarket said. “Out of an abundance of caution, we have temporarily halted trading & are working to bring the platform back online,” it added. Trading began again at 3 p.m. ET after nearly an hour offline. Polymarket’s U.S.-based platform did not appear to be affected by the breach. Polymarket was valued at $21 billion in September after a group of investors led by Donald Trump Jr. invested $1 billion into the platform. The platform, along with rival Kalshi, have become to subject of an intense, multi-million-dollar battle between U.S. states and the Trump administration over who gets to regulate the prediction-market betting that occurs on the sites. The platforms also continue to fight off insider-trading threats. Earlier Thursday, Bloomberg News reported Polymarket was investigating reports of suspicious bets made amid Israel’s closely watched elections. It is also investigating “dozens” related to the U.S. midterms, according to the company’s head of global intelligence and investigations, Shana Bautista. Earlier this month, Kalshi said it was looking into suspicious bets involving Trump’s choice of press secretary.

data.title: Google-parent Alphabet’s stock price plunges, erasing more than $500 billion in value
data.description: Shares of Google parent company Alphabet sank on Thursday by as much as 15.8%, putting the company on course for its worst single-day drop in history. The plunge also instantly wiped out more than $550 billion in market capitalization, also ranking as the company’s worst one day market value loss ever. It also ranks as the second-worst wipeout in market history, only behind Nvidia’s $589 billion drop in 2025. Google is still America’s fourth largest company by market value, and its shares are worth more than $3.4 trillion, all told. But the sharp drop in its stock price Thursday was the latest sign of a broader anxiety creeping through Wall Street over how long it will take big artificial intelligence companies to see consistent returns on their massive investments. The significant selling came after the company reported its latest quarterly financials Wednesday, revealing that revenues fell short of Wall Street expectations. It also reported lackluster advertising sales. The “magnitude” of the slowdown in Google’s search business was “steeper than expected,” JPMorgan Chase analysts wrote in a Thursday morning note. A senior Alphabet executive told investors Wednesday that part of the reason ad revenues from search were underperforming was because of Google’s own “AI Mode” search feature, which was resulting in fewer ads. The company is working on addressing this, senior vice president Philipp Schindler said on the investor call, adding that “ad experiments” in the feature have “shown promising results” Company executives tried to soften the blow for investors by touting more than 1 billion users of its Gemini AI app. But all that AI is coming at a massive cost to Alphabet, which disclosed that it has committed to more than $1 trillion worth of multi-year spending agreements to fund the infrastructure, energy and leases required to run AI systems. The company said during its July earnings report that it planned to spend more than $200 billion this year, which is double what it spent in 2025. The company in June also raised almost $80 billion in capital, also to spend on the ever-expanding AI buildout. Alphabet’s disappointing results also came against the backdrop of better results from its peer Microsoft, whose shares initially rose in after market trading Wednesday and overnight, before reversing course to fall about 2% by 10:50 a.m. ET Thursday. The big drop in Alphabet shares dragged down the Nasdaq Composite index, which was down 1.6% by mid-morning. The S&P 500 fell slightly less, by about 0.6%. Stock in the chip companies that supply equipment for AI data centers followed Alphabet shares lower, with the Philadelphia semiconductor index dropping 1.6%. The bleeding even spread beyond the tech sector, as shares of construction equipment giant Caterpillar — a key supplier of the machines required to build data centers — plunged 9% early Thursday. Caterpillar’s recent earnings report revealed that the company’s revenues beat Wall Street expectations, but by less than many traders had hoped. As investors clamor for ever-higher returns from companies linked to the costly AI buildout, stock in firms that only narrowly top earnings targets, like Caterpillar, have been punished with dramatic sell-offs.

data.title: Utah charges Kalshi and its founders, escalating a fight over who can regulate prediction markets
data.description: Utah on Wednesday filed criminal charges against prediction market operator Kalshi and two of its executives, months after a federal judge rejected Kalshi's effort to prevent Utah from enforcing its strict anti-gambling laws against the activity. The felony charges could represent a new tactic in how states try to assert regulatory authority over the fast-expanding activity, a clash that appears headed to a showdown at the U.S. Supreme Court. The charges include 13 counts of violating the state's prohibition on gambling and another charge involving profiting off illegal activity. The state's charging documents name Kalshi and its co-founders, chief executive officer Tarek Mansour and chief operating officer Luana Lopes Lara. In a statement, Utah Attorney General Derek Brown said Kalshi has continued to operate in Utah, despite a federal court ruling that Utah's gambling laws apply to the company. “Gambling is illegal in Utah, whether you place the bet, run the game, or promote it. Calling it a ‘prediction market’ doesn’t change what it is, and being federally registered doesn’t put a company above the law," Brown said in a statement. The attorney general's office did not immediately say what sort of criminal penalties it would seek in the case, although the felony charges carry the possibility of jail time. In a statement, Kalshi called the charges a “crazy overreach” and said that “Utah is clearly playing politics.” “We look forward to putting a stop to this in court, just like we did in Arizona,” it said. Utah has been on the front lines of a battle between states and the federal government over who regulates the markets. Litigation has spread across roughly 20 states, creating a fragmented legal landscape that analysts say will likely be settled by the U.S. Supreme Court. Kalshi has maintained that prediction markets fall exclusively under federal jurisdiction and are not governed by state gambling laws. Under President Donald Trump, the federal agency responsible for regulating financial markets, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, has agreed and even sued at least 10 states — including Utah this week — to try to stop states from regulating prediction markets. Arizona earlier this year became the first state to file criminal charges against Kalshi, accusing it of operating an illegal gambling business within its borders. A judge later put that case on hold. But one legal analyst, Daniel Wallach, said Arizona's authority to pursue the misdemeanor charges could soon be restored after the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in San Francisco refused to let Kalshi restart trading on sports and elections events in Nevada while it fights the state’s effort to shut it down. Still, Utah's pursuit of felony charges represents a potential shift in strategy by states that have primarily pursued civil actions against prediction market operators, said Wallach, a lawyer who specializes in sports wagering and gaming law and teaches at the University of Miami School of Law. Wallach said he expects to see states bring more cases like Utah's and that Utah's criminal charges “could be a bellwether for how other states approach Kalshi and Polymarket" following Nevada's appellate court victory. Kalshi sued Utah in February, asking a federal judge to prevent the state from enforcing its gambling restrictions on the platform. The lawsuit came as Utah was on the verge of enacting legislation intended to undercut prediction markets from doing business in the state. A federal judge rejected the request, saying the federal law that Kalshi cited in its argument, the Commodity Exchange Act, doesn't prevent the state from enforcing its laws. The 10th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in Denver last month declined to halt Utah's regulatory enforcement during Kalshi's appeal. Last week, Utah also sued Kalshi and several related companies, asking a state court to stop the platform from trading on sports, elections, politics, culture and other outcomes in Utah, and to use a court-approved geolocation provider to enforce it. The attorney general's office also asked the court to make the defendants give up the profits they made in Utah. ___ Follow Marc Levy at http://twitter.com/timelywriter

data.title: Doordash to acquire Instacart for $17 billion, creating delivery giant
data.description: Delivery giant DoorDash is buying to-your-door grocery service Instacart for $17 billion, the company announced Thursday. The deal means users will be able to order groceries and items from other retailers via DoorDash and its delivery network. The companies said Instacart customers can now shop at more than 50,000 additional stores on top of the nearly 100,000 stores on the Instacart platform today. DashPass and Instacart+ members will now also pay one membership fee instead of two. DoorDash is expected to keep the Instacart brand and its technology. Until the transaction closes, DoorDash and Instacart will continue to operate as separate and independent companies. “Over the last 14 years, Instacart has transformed online grocery by helping retailers of all sizes compete and grow, and joining forces with DoorDash allows us to do even more,” said Chris Rogers, CEO of Instacart. The deal represents the latest chapter of consolidation in the delivery industry. Last year, DoorDash bought UK-based Deliveroo, while Uber now owns Postmates ​and Delivery Hero. DoorDash has emerged as the most successful stand-alone online delivery platform in America, commanding some two-thirds of all food-delivery volumes as of 2024, according to Bloomberg data. But over the past year, the company has seen its share price decline by approximately a third, largely due to rising costs. Instacart, meanwhile, reached the pinnacle of its success during the Covid-19 pandemic, when lockdowns sent millions of consumers to their phones to order up groceries. But the company’s stock has gone nowhere over the past two years, as Instacart struggled to find new paths to growth while facing increasing competition from Amazon and Walmart’s grocery-delivery offerings. While a merger would create cost-savings by allowing the combined company to reduce its corporate workforce and split some expenses, it’s not clear how much more money there remains that can be squeezed out of delivery customers. U.S. at-home eaters have begun to complain about the price of food delivery — and the pinch has only worsened this year amid soaring fuel costs, which have led to new fees and surcharges. A recent debate about the cost of having a burrito delivered went viral, as social media users argued over whether $20 was a reasonable price to pay to have the Tex-Mex treat delivered. Platforms like DoorDash and Instacart have also faced legal scrutiny over how they treat workers who deliver for their respective platforms. Last month, DoorDash settled with New York City regulators for $131.5 million to resolve charges it deprived workers of millions of dollars in tips. “Simply put, we screwed up,” the San ‌Francisco-based ⁠company said in a statement. “Our mistakes meant some Dashers were underpaid or paid late. While these mistakes weren’t intentional, that doesn’t make them okay.” The proposed transaction was first reported by tech website The Information and The Wall Street Journal.
